It should also make clear exactly who the president needed to consult. The panel suggests that the president talk to "a joint Congressional committee made up of the leaders of the House and the Senate as well as the chairmen and ranking members of key committees." The new committee would have a permanent professional staff with access to intelligence information, Baker and Christopher said. Congress, in turn, would have to declare war or vote on a "resolution of approval" within 30 days, they said. If a resolution of approval failed, any member of Congress could introduce a "resolution of disapproval," but it was not clear that such an act would stop a war in progress. Christopher was unable to say in the news conference what practical effect congressional disapproval would have. Baker said the commission had been in touch with the presidential campaigns of Democrat Barack Obama and Republican John McCain, as well as leaders of Congress. He declined to reveal what they thought of the proposal, but said: "We haven't gotten a negative reaction." Congress has not officially declared war since 1942, when the United States entered formal hostilities with the Axis powers in World War II. But since then, presidents have sent troops into countries including Korea, Vietnam, Grenada and Iraq. The Constitution makes the president the commander in chief of the armed forces, but gives Congress the power to declare war and approve military budgets. Baker and Christopher's group included both Republicans and Democrats and held seven meetings over 14 months.

outputs.L1:
WASHINGTON (CNN) — The United States needs a new law requiring the president to consult with Congress before going to war, according to a blue-ribbon panel led by two former secretaries of state, which released its recommendations Tuesday.

James Baker and Warren Christopher led the panel, which recommended replacing the current War Powers Resolution with a new War Powers Act.

The existing War Powers Resolution is “ineffective, and it should be repealed and it should be replaced,” Baker said during a joint appearance with Christopher to announce the results of their study.

The recommendation comes after failed efforts by congressional Democrats to halt the war in Iraq or impose conditions on President Bush’s conduct of it. Congress passed a joint resolution authorizing the use of armed force against Iraq in 2002, but some critics of the Bush administration argue that it should not have been interpreted as a blank check for the United States to invade and occupy the Persian Gulf nation.

Baker, who served in the administration of President George H.W. Bush, and Christopher, who served under President Bill Clinton, said their work was not prompted by any specific war. Christopher added that the commission had “tried very hard not to call balls and strikes on past history here.”

“We didn’t direct this report at any particular conflict,” Baker said.

The current law, the War Powers Resolution of 1973, has been regarded as unconstitutional by every president since it was enacted in response to the Vietnam War, Baker and Christopher said. The resolution requires presidents to report regularly to Congress on ongoing conflicts, but that provision has often been ignored.

“No president has ever made a submission to Congress pursuant to the War Powers Resolution since 1973,” former Sen. Slade Gorton, a Republican member of the committee, said Tuesday.

The panel, formally known as the National War Powers Commission, said a new law should require the president to consult with key members of Congress before sending troops into combat expected to last more than one week, or within three days of doing so in the case of operations that must remain secret.

The law should also specify precisely whom the president must consult. The panel recommended that the president confer with “a joint Congressional committee made up of the leaders of the House and the Senate as well as the chairmen and ranking members of key committees.”

Baker and Christopher said the new committee would have a permanent professional staff with access to intelligence information.

Congress, in turn, would be required to declare war or vote on a “resolution of approval” within 30 days, they said. If such a resolution failed, any member of Congress could introduce a “resolution of disapproval,” though it was not clear whether such a measure would halt a war already in progress.

At the news conference, Christopher was unable to say what practical effect congressional disapproval would have.

Baker said the commission had been in contact with the presidential campaigns of Democrat Barack Obama and Republican John McCain, as well as with congressional leaders. He declined to disclose their views on the proposal, but said, “We haven’t gotten a negative reaction.”

Congress has not formally declared war since 1942, when the United States entered hostilities against the Axis powers in World War II. Since then, however, presidents have sent troops into countries including Korea, Vietnam, Grenada and Iraq.

The Constitution designates the president as commander in chief of the armed forces, while granting Congress the authority to declare war and approve military budgets.

Baker and Christopher’s group included both Republicans and Democrats and held seven meetings over 14 months.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — A high-level bipartisan commission headed by two former U.S. secretaries of state said Tuesday that the country should adopt a new statute requiring presidents to consult Congress before initiating war.

James Baker and Warren Christopher co-chaired the panel, which proposed replacing the existing War Powers Act framework. Speaking alongside Christopher as they released the study’s findings, Baker said the current War Powers Resolution is “ineffective” and should be repealed and substituted with a new law.

The proposal comes after congressional Democrats unsuccessfully tried to end the Iraq War or place restrictions on President George W. Bush’s handling of it. In 2002, Congress approved a joint resolution authorizing the use of military force against Iraq, but some critics of Bush have argued that the measure should not have been treated as unlimited permission for the United States to invade and occupy the Persian Gulf country.

Baker, who served in the administration of President George H.W. Bush, and Christopher, who served under President Bill Clinton, emphasized that their work was not aimed at any single conflict. Christopher said the commission had “tried very hard not to call balls and strikes on past history here.” Baker similarly stated, “We didn’t direct this report at any particular conflict.”

According to Baker and Christopher, every president since the War Powers Resolution was enacted in 1973, in the aftermath of the Vietnam War, has viewed the law as unconstitutional. The measure requires presidents to keep Congress informed about continuing military engagements, but that requirement has often been ignored.

“No president has ever made a submission to Congress pursuant to the War Powers Resolution since 1973,” former Sen. Slade Gorton, a Republican member of the commission, said Tuesday.

The group, officially known as the National War Powers Commission, recommended a new law obligating the president to confer with senior congressional figures before committing U.S. forces to combat expected to continue for more than seven days. For secret operations, the president would have to consult Congress within three days after the action began.

The proposed law would also specify exactly which lawmakers must be consulted. The commission recommended that the president meet with “a joint Congressional committee made up of the leaders of the House and the Senate as well as the chairmen and ranking members of key committees.”

Baker and Christopher said that committee would be supported by a permanent professional staff and would have access to intelligence materials.

Under the commission’s plan, Congress would then be required within 30 days either to declare war or vote on a “resolution of approval.” If that approval measure did not pass, any lawmaker could offer a “resolution of disapproval,” although it was uncertain whether such a step would actually halt an ongoing war. At the news conference, Christopher could not explain what concrete consequences congressional disapproval would have.

Baker said the commission had contacted the presidential campaigns of Democrat Barack Obama and Republican John McCain, as well as congressional leaders. He would not disclose their views on the proposal, but said, “We haven’t gotten a negative reaction.”

The United States has not formally declared war since 1942, when it entered official hostilities against the Axis powers during World War II. Since that time, however, presidents have deployed U.S. troops to places such as Korea, Vietnam, Grenada and Iraq.

The Constitution designates the president as commander in chief of the armed forces, while assigning Congress the authority to declare war and approve military spending.

Baker and Christopher’s commission included members from both major political parties and met seven times over a 14-month period.

A bipartisan National War Powers Commission, led by former Secretaries of State James Baker and Warren Christopher, recommended a major overhaul of the way the United States decides when to use military force. The commission urged Congress to repeal the 1973 War Powers Resolution, a law passed in the aftermath of the Vietnam War to limit the president’s ability to involve the country in armed conflict without congressional approval. In its place, the panel proposed a new statute that would require presidents to consult with congressional leaders before launching any significant military operation.

The commission concluded that the existing War Powers Resolution has failed to achieve its purpose. Although the law was intended to restore Congress’s constitutional role in decisions about war, presidents from both parties have often treated it as an unconstitutional restriction on their authority as commander in chief. As a result, the law has been widely ignored, inconsistently followed, and frequently disputed.

Under the commission’s proposed reform, the president would be required to seek meaningful consultation with Congress before initiating major military action, except in emergencies requiring immediate response. The goal would not be to eliminate presidential flexibility in times of crisis, but to ensure that the legislative branch is involved in consequential decisions about the use of force.

The panel argued that such a change would create a clearer and more workable constitutional balance between Congress and the White House. The Constitution gives Congress the power to declare war, while the president serves as commander in chief of the armed forces. In practice, however, modern presidents have often taken the lead in military decisions, leaving Congress with a diminished role.

By replacing the disputed 1973 law with a more practical consultation requirement, the commission hoped to reduce conflict between the branches of government and increase accountability when the nation considers going to war. Its recommendations were significant because they acknowledged both the need for presidential decisiveness and the importance of congressional participation in one of the most serious decisions a government can make.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about a bipartisan commission led by James Baker and Warren Christopher recommending that the 1973 War Powers Resolution be repealed and replaced with a law requiring presidents to consult Congress before going to war.
counterfactuals.output:
**Bipartisan panel urges overhaul of War Powers law**

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — A bipartisan commission led by two former secretaries of state is recommending that Congress repeal the 1973 War Powers Resolution and replace it with a new law requiring presidents to consult with lawmakers before sending U.S. forces into significant armed conflict.

The panel, co-chaired by James Baker, who served as secretary of state under President George H.W. Bush, and Warren Christopher, who held the post under President Bill Clinton, said the current law has failed to provide a workable framework for decisions about war and peace.

The commission’s proposed replacement, known as the War Powers Consultation Act, would require the president to consult with congressional leaders before committing U.S. troops to combat operations expected to last more than a week, except in emergencies. It would also create a permanent congressional committee to meet regularly with the White House on matters involving the use of military force.

The 1973 War Powers Resolution was enacted after the Vietnam War, over President Richard Nixon’s veto, as an effort by Congress to reclaim authority over military commitments. It requires presidents to notify Congress within 48 hours of deploying troops into hostilities and generally requires forces to be withdrawn after 60 days unless Congress authorizes the action.

But presidents of both parties have questioned the resolution’s constitutionality and have often complied with it only in limited ways. The Baker-Christopher commission concluded that the law has been largely ineffective and has done little to ensure meaningful consultation between the executive branch and Congress.

“The current system is broken,” the commission said in its report, arguing that a clearer process is needed to promote cooperation while preserving the president’s ability to respond quickly to threats.

Under the proposal, Congress would be required to vote within 30 days on whether to approve significant military action. If lawmakers failed to act, the president would not automatically be forced to withdraw troops, but members of Congress could use expedited procedures to bring the matter to a vote.

Supporters of the plan say it would encourage presidents to seek congressional backing before military commitments and give lawmakers a more consistent role in national security decisions. Critics may argue that the proposal lacks strong enforcement provisions and could give presidents too much leeway.

The commission included former officials and lawmakers from both parties. Its recommendations come amid long-running debates over the balance of war-making authority between Congress, which has the constitutional power to declare war, and the president, who serves as commander in chief.

Any change to the War Powers Resolution would require approval by Congress and the president’s signature.

It also would establish a permanent congressional consultation committee made up of top House and Senate leaders and the chairmen and ranking members of key national security committees.

Under the proposal, a president would have to report to Congress within three days after the start of a significant conflict. Congress would then be required to vote within 30 days on a resolution of approval. If lawmakers failed to approve the action, they could vote on a resolution of disapproval, though the proposal does not include an automatic cutoff of funds or a mandatory troop withdrawal deadline.

The commission released its recommendations amid continuing debate over the Iraq war and the balance of war-making authority between the White House and Capitol Hill. Baker, who served as secretary of state under President George H.W. Bush, said the proposal was intended to force meaningful consultation without undermining the president’s ability to act quickly in a crisis. Christopher, secretary of state under President Bill Clinton, said the 1973 law had become ineffective and was widely disregarded. He said the commission sought a practical compromise that would respect the president’s role as commander in chief while ensuring Congress has a clear and timely voice.

He said a more structured consultation process might not guarantee different outcomes, but it would make both branches more accountable before the country goes to war.

The commission said its proposal would apply to substantial combat operations expected to last more than a week, while excluding covert actions and limited missions such as training exercises or humanitarian operations. **Panel urges presidents to consult Congress before military action**

A bipartisan blue-ribbon panel is recommending that future presidents seek meaningful congressional input before launching significant military operations, arguing that decades of executive-led interventions have blurred the Constitution’s division of war powers.

The panel’s report calls for a renewed commitment to consultation between the White House and Capitol Hill, particularly when U.S. forces could be placed in harm’s way for sustained operations. While acknowledging that presidents must be able to respond swiftly to imminent threats, the panel says major military action should not rest solely on executive authority when time allows for congressional involvement.

At the center of the debate is the War Powers Resolution, the 1973 law passed in the aftermath of the Vietnam War to check unilateral presidential war-making. The law requires presidents to notify Congress after introducing U.S. forces into hostilities and generally directs that troops be withdrawn within 60 to 90 days unless Congress authorizes the mission or declares war.

But presidents of both parties have long questioned the measure’s constitutionality and often interpreted its requirements broadly. The panel says that pattern has contributed to a steady shift of war-making authority toward the executive branch.

The Constitution gives Congress the power to declare war, raise and support armies, and fund military operations. The president, meanwhile, serves as commander in chief of the armed forces. That shared structure, the panel argues, was designed to ensure both decisiveness and democratic accountability.

The recommendation arrives against the backdrop of presidential politics and ongoing questions about how a new administration would handle crises abroad. During the 2008 campaign, advisers to both Barack Obama and John McCain addressed the balance between presidential authority and congressional oversight, reflecting broader disagreements over Iraq, counterterrorism operations and the use of force.

Obama’s campaign emphasized restoring constitutional checks and seeking congressional participation in major national security decisions, while also maintaining that the president must act when the country faces an imminent threat. McCain, a longtime advocate of a strong national defense, likewise recognized Congress’ role but stressed the need for presidential flexibility in military emergencies.

The panel does not propose eliminating the president’s ability to act quickly in defense of the nation. Instead, it urges a clearer process for consultation, including earlier briefings for congressional leaders, more explicit requests for authorization when military operations are expected to continue, and a more serious role for Congress in debating the scope and goals of force.

Supporters of the recommendation say it could help restore public trust and ensure that military commitments carry broader political legitimacy. Critics warn that requiring congressional input could slow decision-making or politicize urgent security matters.

Still, the panel concludes that the current system too often leaves Congress reacting after military action is already underway. Rebalancing the process, it says, would better reflect the constitutional framework and the gravity of decisions that send Americans into conflict.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize as a full news story the findings of a bipartisan panel led by former Secretaries of State James Baker and Warren Christopher on reforming U.S. war powers law after disputes over Iraq.
counterfactuals.output:
A bipartisan commission led by former Secretaries of State James A. Baker III and Warren Christopher called for a major overhaul of the nation’s war powers law, saying the 1973 War Powers Resolution has failed to provide a workable balance between presidential authority and congressional oversight in decisions to send U.S. forces into combat.

The panel, formed after years of dispute over the Iraq war and broader tensions between Congress and the White House, concluded that the existing law is widely ignored, constitutionally disputed and ineffective in forcing genuine consultation before military action. It recommended replacing the War Powers Resolution with a new statute, the proposed **War Powers Consultation Act**, designed to require presidents and congressional leaders to consult more directly before the United States enters “significant armed conflict.”

Baker, a Republican who served under Presidents Ronald Reagan and George H.W. Bush, and Christopher, a Democrat who served under President Bill Clinton, said the issue should not be treated as a partisan fight over any one war or president. Instead, they argued, the country needs a clearer process for decisions that can place American troops in harm’s way.

The commission found that every president since the War Powers Resolution was enacted has questioned its constitutionality or avoided fully complying with it. The 1973 law requires the president to notify Congress within 48 hours of introducing U.S. forces into hostilities and generally to withdraw them within 60 to 90 days unless Congress authorizes the action. But the panel said that framework has not worked as intended, partly because presidents resist its limits and Congress often avoids taking clear votes on military commitments.

Under the commission’s proposal, the president would be required to consult with a new bipartisan congressional committee before ordering troops into significant combat operations, except in emergencies. That committee would include senior leaders from both parties and key national security committees. If prior consultation were not possible, the president would have to consult within three days after military action began.

The proposal would not give Congress an automatic veto over military operations, nor would it eliminate the president’s ability to respond to sudden attacks or emergencies. But it would require Congress to vote within 30 days on whether to approve significant armed conflict. If lawmakers rejected authorization, they would be expected to vote on a resolution of disapproval. The goal, the commission said, was to force political accountability on both branches rather than allow either to evade responsibility.

The panel defined “significant armed conflict” as combat operations lasting, or expected to last, more than a week. It excluded limited missions such as training exercises, humanitarian operations, covert actions and intelligence activities.

The commission’s recommendations reflected long-running disputes sharpened by the Iraq war, including arguments over whether Congress had been adequately informed, whether the 2002 authorization for force was too broad, and whether lawmakers had surrendered too much authority to the executive branch. The panel said those controversies demonstrated the need for a process that would encourage early, serious consultation rather than after-the-fact political battles.

Baker and Christopher emphasized that war powers are shared under the Constitution: Congress has the power to declare war and fund the military, while the president is commander in chief. The challenge, they said, is to create a practical mechanism that respects both roles in an era when conflicts often begin without formal declarations of war.

The commission’s report did not settle the constitutional debate over who has the final authority to initiate military action. But it sought to reduce ambiguity by replacing a law many officials view as obsolete with one built around consultation, transparency and mandatory votes.

Supporters of reform said the recommendations could help prevent future conflicts from unfolding without broad political consensus. Critics, however, warned that any new statute might still leave presidents with too much freedom or, conversely, could constrain necessary military flexibility.

The report’s central conclusion was that the current system is broken: presidents often act first, Congress often complains later, and the public is left without a clear understanding of who is responsible for taking the country to war. The Baker-Christopher panel urged Congress and the White House to adopt a new framework before the next crisis forces the question again.

counterfactuals.output:
WASHINGTON, July 8 — A bipartisan group of former senior government officials proposed Tuesday that Congress repeal the War Powers Resolution, the post-Vietnam law intended to check a president’s ability to send U.S. forces into combat, and replace it with a new framework requiring regular consultation between the White House and congressional leaders before and during significant military operations.

The proposal, issued by the National War Powers Commission, would create a permanent congressional consultation committee and establish procedures for the president to seek legislative approval for major armed conflicts expected to last more than a week. The commission was led by former Secretary of State James A. Baker III, a Republican, and former Secretary of State Warren Christopher, a Democrat.

The recommendation reflects a long-running frustration in both parties: presidents have often regarded the 1973 War Powers Resolution as an unconstitutional intrusion on their powers as commander in chief, while lawmakers have complained that successive administrations have evaded or ignored the law’s central requirements.

The commission said the existing statute has failed to produce either meaningful consultation or clear constitutional boundaries.

“After 35 years, it is clear that the War Powers Resolution has not worked as intended,” the panel said in its report. “No president has recognized its constitutionality, and Congress has often failed to insist upon its prerogatives.”

The War Powers Resolution was enacted over President Richard Nixon’s veto in 1973, near the end of the Vietnam War, when Congress sought to reassert its authority after years of expanding U.S. military involvement in Southeast Asia. The Constitution gives Congress the power to declare war, raise and support armies, provide and maintain a navy, and regulate the armed forces. It also designates the president as commander in chief of the armed forces.

That division of authority has produced recurring disputes since the nation’s founding, but the Vietnam War transformed the debate. Presidents John F. Kennedy, Lyndon B. Johnson and Nixon deepened U.S. involvement in Vietnam without a formal declaration of war. Johnson relied heavily on the 1964 Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, which authorized the president to take “all necessary measures” to repel attacks and prevent further aggression in Southeast Asia. Critics later argued that Congress had effectively ceded its war-making authority.

The War Powers Resolution was designed to prevent a repeat of that experience. It requires the president to consult with Congress “in every possible instance” before introducing U.S. forces into hostilities, to report such deployments within 48 hours, and to withdraw forces within 60 to 90 days unless Congress authorizes the action or declares war.

But presidents of both parties have submitted reports “consistent with” the resolution rather than “pursuant to” it, language intended to avoid acknowledging that the statute is binding. Military operations in Lebanon, Grenada, Panama, Kosovo, Somalia, Libya and elsewhere have tested the law’s reach.

The 2003 invasion of Iraq added new urgency to the debate. Congress did not declare war, but it passed the 2002 Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq, permitting President George W. Bush to use force to enforce U.N. resolutions and address the perceived threat posed by Saddam Hussein’s government. The administration argued that the authorization, combined with the president’s commander-in-chief powers, provided ample legal basis for the war.

Supporters of the Iraq authorization said Congress had exercised its constitutional role by voting before major combat began. Opponents said the broad authorization illustrated how modern presidents can secure open-ended approvals that fall short of a formal declaration of war but still enable large-scale conflict.

Formal declarations of war have become rare in American history. Congress has declared war only 11 times in five conflicts: the War of 1812, the Mexican-American War, the Spanish-American War, World War I and World War II. Since 1945, presidents have sent U.S. forces into major conflicts — including Korea, Vietnam, the Persian Gulf, Afghanistan and Iraq — without formal declarations, relying instead on U.N. commitments, treaty obligations, congressional authorizations or inherent executive authority.

The commission’s proposed replacement, called the War Powers Consultation Act, would abandon the War Powers Resolution’s automatic withdrawal mechanism. Instead, it would require the president to consult with a new Joint Congressional Consultation Committee before ordering “significant armed conflict,” except in emergencies. The committee would include top leaders from both parties and the chairs and ranking members of relevant national security committees.

Under the proposal, the president would have to provide information on the mission’s objectives, legal basis, expected scope, estimated duration and likely costs. If consultation before the operation were not possible, the president would be required to consult within three days.

For conflicts expected to last more than seven days, the president would be required to submit a report to Congress and seek approval. Congress would then be expected to vote up or down on the operation within 30 days. The plan would provide expedited procedures for such votes, limiting the ability of lawmakers to avoid taking a position.

Unlike the 1973 law, however, the proposal would not force troop withdrawal if Congress failed to act. The commission said that feature of the War Powers Resolution had contributed to constitutional conflict and practical confusion.

Baker and Christopher said the goal was not to favor either branch of government but to make both more accountable.

The president, they argued, must retain the ability to respond quickly to attacks, threats and emergencies. But Congress, they said, should not be sidelined when the nation enters sustained armed conflict.

The proposal also attempts to address one of the central ambiguities in U.S. war powers law: the meaning of “hostilities.” The War Powers Resolution applies when U.S. forces are introduced into hostilities or situations where hostilities are imminent, but administrations have interpreted that term narrowly at times. The commission’s framework would instead focus on “significant armed conflict,” defined to exclude covert operations, limited rescue missions, training exercises and certain actions by special operations forces.

Legal scholars said the proposal reflects the reality that neither branch has been able to impose a decisive interpretation of the Constitution. Courts have generally avoided resolving war powers disputes, often dismissing lawsuits on procedural grounds or treating them as political questions better left to the elected branches.

The president’s commander-in-chief role has been understood to include authority to direct military operations and repel sudden attacks. But Congress’s powers over declarations of war, funding and regulation of the armed forces give it substantial leverage. The unresolved question has been how much unilateral authority a president has to initiate military action without prior congressional approval.

Supporters of a new statute say clearer procedures could reduce the chance that presidents will act alone or that lawmakers will criticize military action while avoiding responsibility for authorizing or opposing it. Critics may object that the proposal weakens Congress by removing the War Powers Resolution’s withdrawal deadline, while others may argue it still intrudes on executive power.

The commission’s plan would require legislation, and its prospects in Congress were uncertain. Lawmakers have frequently debated war powers in the abstract but have been reluctant to constrain presidents of their own party or to cast difficult votes on ongoing military operations.

Still, the report arrives at a moment when the legacy of Vietnam and the continuing consequences of the Iraq war have renewed scrutiny of how the United States decides to use force. The commission said any durable solution must recognize both constitutional principles and modern security demands.

“The country will be better served,” the report said, “if the president and Congress consult meaningfully and if both branches share responsibility for decisions that may place American forces in harm’s way.”
